notes:
I found verse-by-verse comment on all 21 verses. Some sources go deeper than others; gaps are listed at the end.

# Notes on 2 Chronicles 31

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Precept Austin points to the repeated word "all": the people as a whole cleared the land of idols, not just one king. It notes that the reform even reached parts of the old northern kingdom (Ephraim and Manasseh). https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- The order matters. First came turning back to God at the Passover (ch. 30), then the outward cleansing of the land (ch. 31). Precept Austin sums it up as revival moving from worship to obedience in daily life. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- Matthew Henry, quoted there: they spared nothing, however old, costly or popular. His point is that people who really oppose sin oppose all of it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- J. Parker, also quoted there, stresses the word "utterly." Cutting the tops off weeds is not enough; you have to pull up the root. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- Dillard: the reform spread outward in rings, from the temple to the city to the countryside and into parts of the North. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- Utley describes the objects destroyed: pillars (stones linked with Baal worship), Asherah poles (carved or planted trees), high places (raised stone platforms) and probably incense altars. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- Adam Clarke, quoted by Guzik, says we can't tell whether the work in the North came from religious zeal or had the consent of Hoshea, Israel's king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Selman, also quoted by Guzik: the king's earlier removal of idols now became a movement of the people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Hezekiah did not let the Passover be a one-off event. He followed it with regular, organised priestly service. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Guzik quotes Payne: Hezekiah restored the 24 rotating groups ("courses") of priests first set up by David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- The Pulpit Commentary says this amounts to re-establishing courses that had fallen out of order (described in 1 Chronicles 24–26). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/31-2.htm
- Gill: the courses were fixed by David, kept under Jehoshaphat, then interrupted until Hezekiah restored them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/31-2.htm
- "Gates of the camp of the LORD": the Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew word is "camps," not "tents." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/31-2.htm
- Duguid: the phrase calls back to the wilderness tabernacle, showing continuity with Israel's past. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- Trapp: the temple is fitly called a camp because of the guard the priests kept there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Walton: the priests looked after the offerings and the Levites led the worship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64214/

**v. 3**
- Pulpit Commentary: Hezekiah did not dodge his own share. His portion was the tithe, and he was a very wealthy man. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-31.html
- Dillard: like David and Solomon, Hezekiah gave from his own wealth. The Chronicler likes to show that generous kings prompt generous people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- Guzik later notes Hezekiah often used his riches well, as here, but sometimes handled wealth foolishly (2 Kings 20). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/

**v. 4**
- Guzik: this was a command, not an option. The people were to keep the Law of Moses by supporting the priests with tithes (Numbers 18:21–24). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Guzik: the support freed the Levites to study and teach the Law. He compares Paul on paying elders who teach (1 Timothy 5:17–18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Pulpit Commentary: the command was binding because it was God's ordinance through Moses, not simply because the king said it. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-31.html
- Precept Austin: the order may have gone to Jerusalem's residents because they lived closest to the temple. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary

**v. 5**
- Benson offers two readings of "as soon as the order went out": either news of it spread, or the king widened it to the whole kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/2_chronicles/31.htm
- "Honey": Benson says Jewish writers usually took the word to mean dates here. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/2-chronicles-31.html
- The Pulpit Commentary disagrees and says the word is the normal one for bees' honey. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-31.html
- Selman, quoted by Guzik: firstfruits belonged to the priests, while tithes went to the Levites. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Kingcomments: God's word reached the people's hearts, and that is where the willingness to give comes from. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/2-chronicles-31.html
- Precept Austin's application: giving God the first and best, not leftovers, shows gratitude and trust. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64214/

**v. 6**
- "Tithe of the holy things": Selman (via Guzik) thinks this may be what the Levites passed on to the priests from what they received. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- The Pulpit Commentary links it to the "heave offerings" of Numbers 18:8. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-31.html
- Ellicott: the Hebrew says literally "made heaps heaps," meaning many heaps. He also notes the Greek translation misread "holy things" as "goats." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/31-6.html
- Precept Austin adds that tithes were also meant for foreigners, orphans and widows (Deuteronomy 14:29). https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64214/

**v. 7**
- Pulpit Commentary: the grain harvest ended with the Feast of Weeks in the third month. The seventh month brought the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the grape harvest. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-31.html
- Precept Austin: the four months covered every main crop, from barley and wheat to grapes, dates and olives. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64214/
- Guzik: so much was given that receiving it all took four months. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/

**v. 8**
- Poole (via Guzik): they blessed God both for a rich harvest and for giving the people generous hearts. Guzik adds that it showed God's Spirit at work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Precept Austin: the heaps were a visible sign of revival, not just of wealth. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64214/

**v. 9**
- Keil & Delitzsch: Hezekiah was not asking whether there was enough. He wanted to know how such huge piles had built up. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/31-6.html
- Precept Austin: "questioned" can sound hostile, but more likely the king wondered whether the priests had actually been taking their share. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary

**v. 10**
- Precept Austin: the chief priest's answer meant the clergy were well fed and the heaps were the surplus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- Guzik: the long-neglected priests now had plenty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Matthew Henry (via Precept Austin): church funds should not be hoarded longer than needed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary

**v. 11**
- Matthew Henry: the gifts were stored safely, not left in open heaps where they could be wasted or stolen. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/31-20.html
- Guzik: good management honours both God and the givers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/

**vv. 12–13**
- Guzik: Hezekiah put trustworthy men in charge, with overseers to keep them accountable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew word for "faithfully" stresses how much trust the job required. It may hint that the duty had not always been done honestly before. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-31.html
- Ellicott: "the contributions" means the heave offering, which here seems to be the firstfruits of v. 5. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/31-12.html

**vv. 14–15**
- Matthew Henry: officers of proven wisdom handed out the gifts so every priest's family had enough. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- Pulpit Commentary: the gifts were so plentiful they were even called "freewill offerings." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-31.html

**v. 16**
- This is the hardest verse. Ellicott treats it as an aside naming an exception. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/31-16.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: priests serving at the temple were left out of the local handout because their temple duty already fed them and their children. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/31-16.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch agree and conclude that serving priests took their sons aged three and up with them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/31-16.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: children under three were probably left off as too young for solid food. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/31-16.htm
- Gill, citing Kimchi: boys under three were not fit to come into the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/31-16.htm
- Kingcomments: priests on duty were fed in Jerusalem, with their children aged three and up. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/2-chronicles-31.html

**v. 17**
- Clarke (via Guzik): Moses set the Levites' starting age at 30; David lowered it to 20. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Kingcomments: the family records stopped anyone posing as a priest to get a share. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/2-chronicles-31.html

**v. 18**
- Matthew Henry, citing Bishop Patrick: the priests served "in faith," trusting they would be provided for, so care was taken that their hope was not disappointed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_031.cfm
- Poole (via Guzik): wives and children were supported because the priests had given up worldly work to serve. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- Ellicott: the main story, paused after v. 15, picks up again here. The Bible Hub study notes stress that children were counted as members of the covenant. https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/31-18.htm

**v. 19**
- Kingcomments: priests living out in the country were not forgotten, as long as they were in the records. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/2-chronicles-31.html

**v. 20**
- Matthew Henry: Hezekiah's zeal reached every part of the kingdom, not just the area near him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_031.cfm
- The Expositor's Bible Commentary (via Precept Austin): Hezekiah's reign is marked by steady obedience to God's law. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary

**v. 21**
- G. Campbell Morgan: the verse shows Hezekiah's purpose ("to seek his God," like "seek first the kingdom"), his method (with all his heart) and the result (success in the very work he attempted). https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64214/
- Precept Austin: he prospered not only in money or politics but above all spiritually. Blessing does not always come in worldly terms. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64214/
- Duguid: the verse teaches that seeking the Lord and keeping his law lead to prospering. It was a model for the community after the exile. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-31-commentary
- Pulpit Commentary: half-hearted efforts only produce feeble results. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-31.html
- Spurgeon and F. B. Meyer both preached on this verse as a call to serve with the whole heart. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64214/

## 2. Where Protestants differ: must Christians tithe? (vv. 4–6, 12)

The sources below mostly don't name their denomination, so I've grouped them by position rather than by church. Readers shouldn't assume any one view belongs to a whole tradition.

**Not required (generous, free giving instead)**
- Thomas Schreiner (The Gospel Coalition): Christians are not under the covenant of Moses, there are no Levites now, and the New Testament never mentions tithing when it tells people to give. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/7-reasons-christians-not-required-to-tithe/
- John Piper (Desiring God): the tithe was God's way of supporting the Levitical priesthood, so it ended with that system. He expects free, joyful giving to often go beyond a tenth. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/can-a-church-require-tithing
- GotQuestions: no percentage is required, but regular giving in proportion to income is. https://www.gotquestions.org/tithing-Christian.html
- Bible.org (Steven Cole): tithing can feel like paying dues, when in fact everything we have belongs to God. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-4-why-you-should-not-tithe-selected-scriptures

**Middle position**
- Guzik (Enduring Word): no New Testament command, but tithing came before Moses (Hebrews 7). Ten percent is a good benchmark and starting point. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-31/
- TGC Canada: "no" if "tithe" is meant in the strict technical sense; "yes" if it means generous giving in proportion to your means. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/ad-fontes/are-christians-required-to-tithe/

**Binding**
- A. W. Pink (on CCEL): tithing belongs to the moral law, not the ceremonial law, and is even more binding on Christians than on Israel. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/pink/tithing.iii.html

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship and Bible translations (v. 16)**
- Translations disagree on the age. NASB, LSB, Amplified, ISV and GNT have "thirty"; KJV, ESV, NIV, NET and BSB have "three." https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/31-16.htm
- Kingcomments notes that "three" is what the Hebrew says. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/2-chronicles-31.html
- Ellicott dated Chronicles to around 330–300 BC, after Ezra and Nehemiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles.html

**Prosperity teaching (vv. 10, 21)**
- No source applied this chapter directly to prosperity teaching. The general debate is still relevant, though, because of "the LORD has blessed his people" and "he prospered."
- An Assemblies of God (Pentecostal) journal published a biblical evaluation of the teaching. It defines it as the belief that wealth comes through positive confession and "sowing seeds" by paying tithes and offerings. https://enrichmentjournal.ag.org/Issues/2015/Winter-2015/The-Prosperity-Gospel-A-Biblical-Evaluation
- Critics at TGC say the teaching ignores that promises of material blessing belong to the old covenant. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/3-things-your-bible-doesnt-say-about-money/
- Catholic Answers (Trent Horn) calls the "give to get" idea a way of trying to manipulate God. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/why-the-prosperity-gospel-is-bankrupt

**Not found**
- NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, Catholic or Orthodox comment on this chapter itself, and Lutheran or Methodist writers (including Wesley's notes).
- The short Douay-Rheims (Catholic) wording of v. 16 is the only Catholic item. https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/31-16.htm
